newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea arrests three more unionists in crackdown.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea arrests three more unionists in crackdown.

text.p: South Korean police arrested three more strike leaders in a crackdown on labour strife, but unions on Thursday defiantly threatened to prolong the stoppages for another two months.
Prosecution officials said police arrested three shipyard unionists at Halla Heavy Industries during the night on charges of obstructing business.

This brings to four the number of union heads seized. Unionists have braced for a crackdown since a warning by the country's top prosecutor that North Korea may be fanning industrial unrest to try to topple the government.
The three were also accused of beating up workers who refused to down tools at the shipyard in the southwestern town of Yongam, a prosecution official said.
Another Halla Heavy union leader was arrested on Tuesday night on similar charges, the official said.

The president of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, Kwon Young-kil, said authorities had stoked worker fury with their handling of the three-week strikes, sparked by the passage of a new labour law.

"The confederation could prolong the current strikes for more than two months," Kwon told reporters at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral where he and six other confederation leaders are sheltering from arrest.
Meanwhile, four international labour leaders left South Korean under a cloud after deportation warnings by authorities angry at what they viewed as outside meddling in the strikes.
The four had attracted intense local media coverage with visits to Myongdong Cathederal and by appearing on stage as star guests at worker rallies.

A British member of the team was due to report to the Organisation for Economic Coooeration and Development (OECD) on the new law, which allows companies to lay off workers, and on threats against union leaders.
The OECD, which South Korea joined last December, has scheduled a meeting on January 22 to review the legislation.
Some members of the Paris-based group believe the law violates worker rights to freedom of expression by maintaining a ban on new union bodies until 2000.
The confederation has warned authorities of all-out strikes if its seven leaders at Myongdong are arrested.
"We seriously warn that they are repeating the serious misjudgement they showed when they railroaded the evil labour law," Kwon told reporters.
The law was rammed through parliament on December 26 by the ruling New Korea Party in the absence of opposition deputies.

A general strike called on Tuesday and Wednesday by the officially recognised Federation of Korean Trade Unions and the confederation fizzled out, although there were violent clashes in central Seoul between riot police and thousands of rock-throwing workers.
On Thursday, the chairman of the ruling New Korea Party, Lee Hong-koo, expressed "humble regret" for the way the legislation was adopted but ruled out any revisions.

"I would like to use this occasion to make known again my willingness to resolve all problems through dialogue and compromise," Lee told a news conference. He promised steps to allay worker fears the law could lead to layoffs.

Arrest warrants are outstanding for a total of 16 union leaders, including the seven at the cathedral. Domestic media reports said arrests were imminent, but prosecutors were not immediately available for comment.
Confederation affiliates were still staging scattered industrial action across the country, although transport and key services were all operating normally on Thursday.
The outlawed umbrella body said 350,000 members had walked out. The labour ministry put the figure at 67,000 out of a workforce of 12 million.

In the southeast city of Ulsan, a traditonal hotbed of union militancy, about 10,000 striking Hyundai workers staged a noisy sit-in protest outside Hyundai Heavy Industries, the country's biggest shipyard.
Dockyard worers on Wednesday smashed through picket lines to keep the giant facility open.
